extraction.name: AMASS
extraction.description: A large and varied database of human motion that unifies 15 different optical marker-based mocap datasets by representing them within a common framework and parameterization using SMPL body models. The dataset contains more than 40 hours of motion data, spanning over 300 subjects and more than 11000 motions.
extraction.creator: Naureen Mahmood, Nima Ghorbani, Nikolaus F. Troje, Gerard Pons-Moll, Michael J. Black
extraction.rai:dataCollection: AMASS unifies 15 different optical marker-based motion capture datasets by converting them into a common SMPL representation using the MoSh++ method. The datasets were obtained from various sources: some were publicly downloaded from the internet, others were obtained privately, and some were recorded by the researchers themselves (Dancers, Transitions, BioMotionLab, and SSM). A new SSM dataset was specifically recorded using an OptiTrack motion capture system with 24 cameras synchronized with a 3dMD 4D body scanning system. Subjects wore 67 reflective markers placed directly on skin with minimal clothing. Results were manually inspected to correct or remove problems like swapped and mislabeled markers.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of optical motion capture marker data from 15 different datasets, each recorded with different numbers of markers placed at different body locations. The SSM dataset specifically includes synchronized 67 reflective marker positions captured at high frame rates along with corresponding 4D body scans from a 3dMD scanning system capable of capturing at 60 frames per second using 22 pairs of stereo cameras.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: MoSh++ method with SMPL-H body model, DMPL for soft-tissue deformations, and MANO hand model
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The method has several limitations including: 1) MoSh relies on a formulation of the SCAPE body model which is not compatible with existing body representations and graphics software; 2) MoSh captures only approximate soft tissue motions represented by changing the identity of a subject over time rather than true soft-tissue deformations; 3) MoSh did not solve for the pose and motion of the hands.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains body shape information from 346 subjects captured through motion capture data, including 3D body shape parameters, soft tissue coefficients, and full body pose parameters including hand articulations.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for animation, visualization, and generating training data for deep learning applications in computer vision and animation. Users can utilize the data for pose estimation, body shape modeling, and can normalize bodies to the same shape if needed for specific applications.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset will be publicly available to the research community and the authors plan to continue expanding the dataset with new captures that can be similarly shared.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The method converts motion capture marker data into 3D human meshes using the SMPL body model through a two-stage fitting process. The preprocessing involves: (1) mapping pose-invariant marker representations to posed frames, (2) fitting body shape, pose, and soft-tissue dynamics parameters to observed mocap markers, (3) recovering skeletal structure with joints and rigged surface mesh, and (4) unifying 15 different optical marker-based mocap datasets with varying markersets (37 to 91 markers) into a common framework and parameterization.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We amassed in total 15 mocap datasets... The publicly available datasets were downloaded from the internet. We obtained several other datasets privately or recorded them ourselves (Dancers, Transitions, BioMotionLab and SSM)... To record this dataset we use an optical motion capture system synchronized and calibrated together with a high resolution 4D scanning system... Due to inherent problems with mocap, such as swapped and mislabeled markers, we manually inspected the results and either corrected or held out problems.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: To record this dataset we use an optical motion capture system synchronized and calibrated together with a high resolution 4D scanning system. We used an OptiTrack motion capture system (NaturalPoint, Inc. DBA OptiTrack. Corvallis, OR) consisting of 24 Optitrack Prime 17W optical mocap cameras. Each subject was fitted with 67 reflective mocap markers

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: Each dataset was recorded using a different number of markers placed at different locations on the body; even within a dataset, the number of markers varies... Each subject was fitted with 67 reflective mocap markers based on the optimized marker-set layout proposed in [27]... The 4D scanner is capable of capturing high-resolution 3D scans of a person at 60 frames per second. The 4D system uses 22 pairs of stereo cameras

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: We achieve this using a new method, MoSh++, that converts mocap data into realistic 3D human meshes represented by a rigged body model; here we use SMPL [28], which is widely used and provides a standard skeletal representation as well as a fully rigged surface mesh... Here we add the recent MANO hand model [36], which is compatible with SMPL, and solve for body and hand pose when hand markers are present... we use the dynamic shape space of DMPL [28], which is leamed from thousands of dynamic scans.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: MoSh employs a generative model of the body, leamed from a large number of 3D body scans, to compute the full 3D body shape and pose from a sparse set of motion capture markers. The results are realistic, but the method has several important limitations, which make it inappropriate for our task. First, MoSh relies on a formulation of the SCAPE body model [13], which is not compatible with existing body representations and graphics software... Second, while MoSh captures some soft tissue motions, these are approximate and represented by changing theidentity of a subject over time; that is, they are not true soft-tissue deformations... Third, MoSh did not solve for the pose and motion of the hands.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: AMASS has42hours of mocap, 346subjects, and 11451 motions... Each frame in AMASS includes the SMPL 3D shape parameters ( 16dimensions), the DMPL soft tissue coefficients ( 8dimensions), and the full SMPL pose parameters ( 90dimensions), including hand articulations.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: The consistent representation of AMASS makes it readily useful for animation, visualization, and generating training data for deep leaming... Users who only care about pose can ignore body shape and soft tissue deformations if they wish. Similarly, the SMPL shape space makes it trivial to normalize all bodies to the same shape if users want joint locations normalized to a single shape.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: We make AMASS available to the research community at http://amass.is.tue.mpg.de , and will support the community in adding new captures as long as they can be similarly shared... With MoSh++ it is easy to add more data and we will continue to expand the dataset.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We achieve this using a new method, MoSh++, that converts mocap data into realistic 3D human meshes represented by a rigged body model... MoSh++ captures body shape, pose, and soft-tissue dynamics by fitting the surface of the SMPL/DMPL body model to observed mocap markers, while also providing a rigged skeleton... We combine 15 existing motion capture datasets into one large dataset... The source datasets all contain varying markersets ranging in size from 37 to 91 markers; AMASS unifies these into a single format.
